title: Encapsulation and Access Control
relevance: SDE interviews probe whether candidates understand Python’s convention-based encapsulation, name mangling, and @property validation versus compiler-enforced access control.

phases.goal: Establish what encapsulation means and that Python uses conventions instead of language keywords for access control.

must_hit.point: Encapsulation bundles data and the methods that operate on it in a class and restricts direct access to some components.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines encapsulation as bundling attributes with methods and limiting direct access to internals.

must_hit.point: Unlike Java or C++, Python has no public/private/protected keywords and relies on conventions and trust (“we are all consenting adults here”).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts compiler-enforced keywords with Python’s convention-and-trust model.

must_hit.point: By default, all attributes and methods in a Python class are public and accessible from anywhere.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states that unmarked members are public and freely accessible.

probes: How does encapsulation in Python differ from languages like Java or C++?

hints.1: Think about whether Python has private or protected keywords.
hints.2: Contrast compiler-enforced access modifiers with naming conventions and trust.
hints.3: Python has no public/private/protected keywords; members are public by default and access is guided by convention (“consenting adults”).

phases.goal: Explain single-underscore and double-underscore naming, including what name mangling actually does.

must_hit.point: A single leading underscore (e.g. _engine_temp) is a convention for internal-use-only members; Python does not prevent access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says _ means “internal; don’t rely on it,” and notes access still works (Staff Only on an unlocked door).

must_hit.point: A double leading underscore (e.g. __serial_number) triggers name mangling: Python rewrites the name to include the class name (e.g. _Car__serial_number).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains mangling to _ClassName__attr and that the bare __name raises AttributeError from outside.

must_hit.point: Name mangling’s primary purpose is avoiding name collisions under inheritance, not securing the attribute.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects “security” as the goal and cites collision avoidance when subclasses inherit.

probes: What happens if you access my_car.__serial_number, and can you still reach that value somehow?

hints.2: Two underscores rename the attribute; think about the mangled form with the class name.
hints.3: __serial_number becomes _Car__serial_number; direct access fails with AttributeError, but the mangled name still works—and that is for inheritance collisions, not security.

phases.goal: Contrast convention-based privacy with enforced accessors and when @property is preferred over Java-style getters/setters.

must_hit.point: Single-underscore “protection” keeps the public API clean and allows debugging inspection without hoops, at the cost of no real access barrier.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate weighs clean API and easy debug access against the fact that anyone can still read the attribute.

must_hit.point: Java-style get_/set_ methods are considered unpythonic; @property makes a method act like an attribute while allowing validation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate prefers attribute-like @property over explicit getter/setter method names.

probes: Why prefer @property over writing get_temperature and set_temperature methods in Python?

hints.1: Think about how client code should read or assign the value.
hints.2: Clients should keep using attribute syntax while you add validation behind the scenes.
hints.3: @property exposes getter/setter as normal attribute access, which is the Pythonic alternative to Java-style get_/set_ methods.

phases.goal: Apply @property for validation and avoid the common setter recursion failure.

must_hit.point: @property plus a setter can validate assignments (e.g. reject temperature below -273.15) while callers still use attribute syntax.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes getter returning internal storage and setter raising on invalid values, with t.temperature = … calling the setter.

must_hit.point: Starting with a public attribute and later switching to @property with the same name avoids rewriting all client code that uses the class.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains the attribute interface stays stable when validation is added via @property.

must_hit.point: Assigning to self.temperature inside the setter (instead of the backing self._temp_c) causes infinite recursion.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the failure: setter re-enters itself via the property name.

probes: If you later need validation on a field that clients already use as a public attribute, how does @property help—and what goes wrong if the setter assigns to the property name itself?

hints.1: Keep the same attribute name for callers.
hints.2: Store the real value on a private-by-convention field; never assign back through the property inside the setter.
hints.3: Add @property/@setter with the same public name so callers need no rewrite; inside the setter write self._temp_c (or similar)—assigning self.temperature recurses forever.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Python signals intent with underscores and trusts callers (“consenting adults”); _ does not block access, and __ only mangles names for inheritance safety—not true privacy—unlike Java/C++ keywords.
Explicit get_/set_ methods are unpythonic; @property keeps attribute syntax for clients while allowing validation and a later switch from a bare public attribute without rewriting call sites.

gotchas.trap: Believing name mangling makes an attribute truly secure or inaccessible.
gotchas.correction: Python renames __serial_number to _Car__serial_number; knowing the class name still allows access. Mangling mainly avoids inheritance name collisions.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a single underscore prevents access.
gotchas.correction: A single underscore is only a convention (Staff Only on an unlocked door); the attribute remains fully accessible.

gotchas.trap: Assigning to self.temperature inside a @temperature.setter instead of the backing field.
gotchas.correction: That re-invokes the setter and causes infinite recursion; assign to the internal store (e.g. self._temp_c).
